core.title: Keep runtime payload values and artifact data out of route declarations
core.given: A plan artifact contains a route declaration (the plan-graph construct that selects routes and declares payload contract identities).
core.when: You write, change or review that route declaration's contents.
core.then: The route declaration selects routes and declares payload contract identities, and contains no runtime payload values and no artifact data.
prefer: Reference each payload by its contract identity and let the route carry the actual payload at runtime.
Keep concrete payload values and artifact content in the payload and artifact definitions where they are produced.
avoid: Inlining runtime payload values (sample or concrete payload data) in any field of a route declaration.
Copying artifact data into a route declaration to 'document' or pre-fill a route.
Hiding runtime payload values in nested or renamed fields to evade the check.
core.why: Route declarations exist to select routes and declare payload contract identities; putting runtime payload values or artifact data in them couples routing to specific payload instances and blurs the boundary between plan and runtime data.
evidence: The stack's check that route declarations reject runtime payload values and artifact data passes for the declaration.
On failure, the finding identifies the offending declaration, the field and the kind of forbidden value; a clean run has no such findings.
verification: Absence check (forbidden-construct absence) over plan artifacts: the route declaration must contain no runtime payload values and no artifact data. What exactly counts as a runtime payload value, a forbidden value kind, or artifact content — including values hidden in nested or renamed fields — is classified by the stack's checker, not by this rule.
Runs in the confirm phase with blocking enforcement; the subject is every route declaration in every plan artifact, whatever its home and whether or not it currently complies.
Per-rule disposition: strict, severity 4. There is no exception and no 'unless' case; a declaration with no forbidden content simply passes.
A failure finding identifies the offending declaration, the field path and the kind of forbidden value; the concrete finding field names are realization details.
Out of scope (what the check does not cover): payload definitions, artifacts and payload contracts outside any route declaration, and plan or acceptance artifacts that contain no route declaration.

fires: Any route declaration is present in a plan artifact, including one that already complies (the rule still applies; it simply passes).
A route declaration contains runtime payload values in some field (applies and fails).
A route declaration contains artifact data in some field (applies and fails).
doesNotFire: Payload definitions, artifacts or payload contracts themselves, outside any route declaration (different subject).
Plan or acceptance artifacts that contain no route declaration (no subject).

neutralityNotes: The rule's subject and data are plan-graph vocabulary, not stack machinery: 'flow router' and 'flow variables' are ATDD-Bun's planner terms. The core uses the functional terms 'route declaration' and 'runtime payload values', and takes the concrete kind name from the proposed profile key idiom.plan_syntax#route_declaration (no existing vocabulary key covers plan-graph declaration constructs). The Bun enumeration in doesNotFire ('Plans, product capabilities, DESIRED OUTCOMES or acceptances') is realization vocabulary; the core keeps the role-level form 'plan or acceptance artifacts that contain no route declaration'. What exactly counts as a runtime payload value, artifact data, or a payload contract identity is not spelled out in bun.json either — the Bun validator classifies it (forbidden_value_kind) — so the core preserves that deference to the stack's checker rather than inventing a definition. The empty 'unless' (strict, no exceptions) is preserved exactly.
